events.title: First Modern Olympics
events.blurb: The first modern Summer Olympic Games opened in an Athens marble stadium built on the foundations of a Panathenaic-festival venue 1,500 years earlier. 241 athletes from 14 nations competed in 43 events over nine days. An amateur Greek water-carrier named Spiridon Louis won the marathon, run along the road from the town to the stadium, and became an instant national hero. A 27-year-old French baron had championed the revival for nearly a decade before the games.
events.revealBlurb: April 6, 1896 — the baron was Pierre de Coubertin. Louis won his race in 2:58:50 carrying a bouquet from his village; his prize included a year's worth of free meals and a plot of land. There were no women athletes; Coubertin considered female participation "impractical, uninteresting, and incorrect."

events.title: First Tour de France
events.blurb: A French sports newspaper, in an effort to increase circulation, organized a 2,428-kilometre bicycle race around the perimeter of France — six stages, each the length of an ultra-endurance event today, with sleep-deprived cyclists riding through the night on dirt roads with a single fixed gear. Sixty cyclists started; only 21 finished. A chimney sweep named Maurice Garin won the inaugural race over 19 days of riding.
events.revealBlurb: July 1-19, 1903 — organized by L'Auto magazine, a forerunner of L'Équipe. Garin's margin of victory was an implausible 2 hours 49 minutes. He was later stripped of his 1904 title for cheating (taking trains). The race continues annually with a couple of wartime interruptions.

events.title: The Rumble in the Jungle
events.blurb: A 32-year-old heavyweight boxing challenger, widely predicted to lose to the younger and vastly more powerful champion, leaned back against the ropes for seven rounds and absorbed punishing body blows — a tactic he later nicknamed "rope-a-dope." In the 8th, when the champion visibly tired, the challenger delivered a flurry of punches that knocked him out. The fight was held in an African capital as part of a pioneering pan-African promotion.
events.revealBlurb: October 30, 1974 — Muhammad Ali KO'd George Foreman at the Stade du 20 Mai in Kinshasa, Zaire (now Democratic Republic of the Congo). Promoter Don King organized it. The event was immortalized in the 1996 documentary "When We Were Kings."

events.title: Magic Johnson Announces HIV
events.blurb: A 32-year-old Lakers star held a nationally televised press conference announcing he would be retiring from the NBA immediately, because he had tested positive for HIV. The announcement — at a moment when the virus was widely associated with gay men and intravenous drug users — instantly changed public perception of who could contract AIDS. He had learned the result days earlier during a routine pre-insurance physical. He would unretire briefly twice, including to play an All-Star Game and the 1992 Olympics.
events.revealBlurb: November 7, 1991 — Earvin "Magic" Johnson at the Los Angeles Forum. He remains alive and visibly healthy over 30 years later, thanks to antiretroviral therapy. His announcement drove huge increases in HIV testing, awareness, and research funding. He returned to the NBA for a 32-game 1995-96 comeback.

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: Great Lisbon Earthquake
events.blurb: On the morning of a major Catholic holy day, a magnitude-9 earthquake struck off the Atlantic coast of a European capital while most residents were at Mass. The quake was followed within 40 minutes by a tsunami that rolled up the Tagus River, and a citywide fire that burned for five days. Roughly 40,000 of the city's 200,000 inhabitants died.
events.revealBlurb: November 1, 1755 — All Saints' Day in Lisbon. Voltaire wrote his anti-optimist poem about it, then Candide. The Portuguese prime minister, the Marquis of Pombal, supposedly asked "What now? We bury the dead and feed the living" and rebuilt the city on a grid.

events.title: Mount Pelée Eruption
events.blurb: A volcanic mountain on a Caribbean island unleashed a pyroclastic flow — a superheated cloud of gas and ash travelling at hurricane speed — that swept down onto the colonial capital below and killed nearly every one of the town's 28,000 inhabitants in about 60 seconds. Two survivors were found: a shoemaker on the outskirts and a prisoner locked in a thick-walled dungeon.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1902 — Saint-Pierre, Martinique. The prisoner, Ludger Sylbaris, was saved by his stone cell, horribly burned but alive. He later joined Barnum & Bailey Circus as "the man who lived through Doomsday."

events.title: Spanish Flu Pandemic Begins
events.blurb: An unusually lethal strain of influenza, carried through military camps and troop ships during the final months of a world war, infected a third of the planet and killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people in three successive waves over two years. Unlike most flus, it disproportionately killed healthy young adults by triggering cytokine storms in robust immune systems.
events.revealBlurb: March 1918 — first identified at a US Army base in Kansas. It was called "Spanish" only because wartime censorship in belligerent countries suppressed coverage; neutral Spain reported it freely, so it seemed to originate there. It had nothing to do with Spain.

events.title: Tōhoku Earthquake & Fukushima
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the Pacific coast of northern Japan triggered tsunami waves up to 40 metres high that killed some 19,700 people and swamped the seawalls of a coastal nuclear plant. Three reactor cores melted down in the following days, contaminating 337 square kilometres of surrounding countryside. 165,000 people were displaced; many never returned.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2011 — 2:46 PM local time. The quake was so powerful it shifted Earth's axis by about 17 centimetres and shortened the day by 1.8 microseconds. The plant's operator, TEPCO, had been warned about tsunami risk years earlier and ignored it.

events.title: Hurricane Sandy
events.blurb: A late-season hurricane merged with a nor'easter over the northeastern US, creating a 1,800-kilometre-wide superstorm whose storm surge flooded subway tunnels, power substations, and lower-Manhattan neighborhoods. 233 people died across eight countries; 8.5 million US households lost electricity. Damages totaled $70 billion.
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 2012 — New Jersey landfall, a week before the US presidential election. Lower Manhattan went dark for four days, producing iconic images of a blacked-out skyline with the Goldman Sachs tower still lit. It pushed climate adaptation into mainstream US infrastructure planning.

events.title: Casablanca Premieres
events.blurb: A wartime romance set in a Moroccan cafe — produced on a tight schedule with an often-improvised script — premiered at a New York theater two weeks after Allied troops actually landed in the real-life city, a coincidence that boosted interest. The film's lead actor and actress had expected it to be a forgettable assignment; its dialogue's half-dozen phrases would be quoted by a century of audiences. Neither of the two stars was anyone's first choice for their parts.
events.revealBlurb: November 26, 1942 — Hollywood Theatre, NYC. Director Michael Curtiz, stars Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman. "Here's looking at you, kid" was Bogart's improvisation. "Play it again, Sam" is never actually said in the film.

events.title: Rashomon Released
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Japanese director released a 88-minute film in which the same violent encounter is recounted by four different participants, none of whom agrees with any of the others. The Venice Film Festival awarded it the Golden Lion the following year, and the world film industry discovered Japanese cinema as a major force. The very title became an English noun: "the Rashomon effect" is the concept of contradictory memories.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1950 — Akira Kurosawa. The producers were reportedly baffled by the script and wanted it re-edited. Its Venice win completely blindsided Japanese critics, who had not thought much of the film. It led directly to the global reception of Ozu, Mizoguchi, and Kurosawa's later work.

events.title: Tokyo Story Released
events.blurb: A Japanese director released a 136-minute film about an elderly provincial couple who travel to the capital to visit their adult children, only to find them too busy with their own lives. Its stationary low-angle camera, dialogues shot face-on toward the audience, and refusal of conventional emotional climax embodied the director's signature style. Polls of international critics and filmmakers regularly rank it among the greatest films ever made.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1953 — Yasujirō Ozu. He developed the "tatami-level" camera position — 30 cm off the ground, corresponding to the height of a person seated on a tatami mat. It did not gain a Western reputation until the 1970s; Ozu had died in 1963, never having lived to see his international recognition.

events.title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial Released
events.blurb: A 35-year-old American director released a 115-minute family film about a stranded alien befriended by a suburban boy who helps him contact his home planet. The director had developed the story as a way of processing his parents' divorce and his imaginary childhood companion. The film topped the box office for 16 weeks, displaced Star Wars as the highest-grossing film of all time, and moved children to tears for decades.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1982 — Steven Spielberg. Composer John Williams won the Oscar for his score; Spielberg himself didn't. The flying-bicycle silhouette against the moon became the logo of Amblin Entertainment, his production company.

events.title: Spirited Away Wins Oscar
events.blurb: A Japanese animated film about a 10-year-old girl's adventure in a bathhouse for spirits won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, an unprecedented achievement for an Asian work in the category. The film's director, then 62, had been making animated features for decades, but most American audiences had never heard of him or his studio. The Oscar made the director a household name and put his studio's catalog on every arthouse wishlist.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2003 — Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli's film won Best Animated Feature. Miyazaki did not attend the ceremony in protest of the Iraq War. "Spirited Away" remains Japan's highest-grossing film and grossed over $395 million worldwide.

events.title: Tutankhamun Death Mask Created
events.blurb: Egyptian craftsmen fashioned a 10.2-kilogram gold funerary mask inlaid with lapis lazuli, carnelian, obsidian, and coloured glass to cover the mummy of a teenage pharaoh who had died at 18. The mask was sealed in a tomb packed with over 5,000 objects. The boy-king had been a minor figure; the tomb escaped the looting that emptied nearly every other Egyptian royal burial. It was untouched for 3,245 years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1323 BCE — Tutankhamun died. Howard Carter's team uncovered the tomb on November 4, 1922. The mask now spends most of its time in a Cairo museum case and has been on world tours twice. The beard fell off during cleaning in 2014 and was hastily reattached with epoxy.

events.title: Bayeux Tapestry Completed
events.blurb: An embroidered strip of linen 70 metres long and 50 centimetres high, worked in coloured wool yarns, depicts in 58 scenes the Norman conquest of a cross-Channel kingdom — the diplomatic prelude, the invasion fleet, a victorious battle, and the death of a king by arrow. It includes 623 human figures, 202 horses, 55 dogs, and a Latin commentary running across the top.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1077 — commissioned either by Bishop Odo of Bayeux or Queen Matilda. Despite its name, it is technically embroidery, not tapestry. It survived the French Revolution only because a local lawyer hid it when a crowd tried to use it to cover an ammunition wagon.

events.title: Van Eyck Paints Arnolfini Portrait
events.blurb: A Flemish painter completed a small oil panel showing an Italian merchant and his wife standing in an upstairs bedroom in a northern European trading city, their hands linked, surrounded by symbolic objects: a burning candle, a tiny dog, a convex mirror reflecting the painter himself. It was among the earliest oil paintings in Europe; the new medium allowed detail and luminosity that tempera could not achieve.
events.revealBlurb: 1434 — Jan van Eyck in Bruges. The couple were Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini and probably his wife. The signature above the mirror is uniquely ostentatious for the period: "Jan van Eyck was here 1434." Now in London's National Gallery.

events.title: Michelangelo's David Unveiled
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Florentine sculptor unveiled a 5.17-metre marble nude of a biblical hero, carved over three years from a single block of Carrara marble that had been rejected by two earlier sculptors as flawed. The statue was intended for the rooftop of a cathedral; a committee that included Leonardo da Vinci decided the work was too significant to put out of sight and instead installed it in the main square of the city.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1504 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. Moving it from the workshop to the Piazza della Signoria took 40 men 4 days. The statue was damaged by a mob in 1527 and by a 1991 attack with a hammer; it now stands indoors at the Accademia, where a copy watches over the piazza.

events.title: Banksy Shreds at Auction
events.blurb: A framed spray-painting of a girl releasing a heart-shaped balloon, sold at a London auction for £1.04 million ten seconds earlier, began to buzz mechanically and slid partway through a concealed shredder built into the custom frame. Half the canvas emerged in vertical strips; the auction house staff stared; the hammer had already fallen. The anonymous street artist who had built the device posted a video saying the mechanism was supposed to shred the whole picture.
events.revealBlurb: October 5, 2018 — Banksy, at Sotheby's London. The buyer honored the purchase. The half-shredded work was retitled "Love is in the Bin" and resold three years later for £18.6 million — 18 times the original price.

events.title: Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: A 78-year-old man, walking slowly across a Delhi lawn supported by two of his grandnieces, was shot three times in the chest at point-blank range by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for indulging Muslims and accepting partition. He fell murmuring the name of a god. He had survived five previous attempts on his life.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1948 — the assassin was Nathuram Godse, a former editor of a Hindu nationalist newspaper. He was convicted and executed. Gandhi had warned his secretary that morning that his life's work would not be judged "until after I am dead and gone."

events.title: Indira Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: The prime minister, walking from her bungalow to a garden office for a scheduled interview with a British filmmaker, was shot 31 times at close range by two of her own Sikh bodyguards. She was rushed to a nearby hospital and died during surgery. Four days of anti-Sikh riots followed in the capital, organized partly by politicians of her own party, killing at least 3,000 people. Her son Rajiv was sworn in as prime minister the same evening.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1984 — Satwant Singh and Beant Singh, bodyguards who had both been retained despite security concerns after Blue Star. The Justice Nanavati Commission documented the organized nature of the subsequent riots; convictions have come only in the last few years.

events.title: Babri Masjid Demolition
events.blurb: A mob of around 150,000 Hindu nationalists who had gathered for what was officially billed as a symbolic prayer ceremony at a disputed 16th-century mosque in a north Indian town overpowered the police cordon and demolished the structure with pickaxes and crowbars over six hours. Riots across the country in the following weeks killed 2,000 people, mostly Muslims. A Hindu temple now stands on the site, inaugurated 31 years later.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1992 — Ayodhya. The Supreme Court ruled in 2019 that the demolition was illegal, but awarded the site to the Hindu temple trust. The Ram Mandir was consecrated on January 22, 2024.

events.title: Pokhran-II Nuclear Tests
events.blurb: India conducted five underground nuclear explosions over two days in the same Rajasthani desert test range it had used 24 years earlier, including a claimed thermonuclear device. The tests, carried out in conditions of extraordinary operational security that surprised American intelligence satellites, declared the country a full nuclear-weapon state. Pakistan tested its own devices 17 days later.
events.revealBlurb: May 11 and 13, 1998 — code-named Operation Shakti. Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee had been in office three months. Sanctions were imposed; they were lifted within two years as the United States reassessed its South Asia policy.

events.title: Demonetisation
events.blurb: In a surprise eight-o'clock television address, the prime minister announced that the two largest-denomination banknotes in circulation — 86 percent of all currency by value — would cease to be legal tender at midnight. The stated targets were counterfeit money, black money, and terrorism financing. Long queues formed outside banks for weeks; small businesses and day-labourers, most paid in cash, were disproportionately hit. Subsequent data showed most demonetised cash returned to the banking system.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 2016 — Narendra Modi. By the Reserve Bank's own accounting, 99.3 percent of the old notes were eventually exchanged. Counterfeit detection was negligible. The policy's effect on corruption is still debated; its effect on GDP was negative.

events.title: Newton's Principia Published
events.blurb: A three-volume work laid out universal laws of motion and gravitation in mathematical form, explaining why apples fall and why planets orbit in ellipses with a single unified framework. The laws held that every mass in the universe attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their distance.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1687 — Edmond Halley paid for the printing out of his own pocket after the Royal Society spent its book budget on a history of fishes. Newton later said a dispute over priority with Robert Hooke was the reason he almost withheld the whole thing.

events.title: Electromagnetic Field Equations Published
events.blurb: A Scottish physicist unified electricity, magnetism, and light into a single mathematical framework of four equations, showing that changing electric fields produce magnetic fields and vice versa — generating self-propagating waves that travel at the speed of light. The equations predicted that light was an electromagnetic wave and implied the existence of radio waves, infrared radiation, and other forms not yet observed.
events.revealBlurb: 1865 — James Clerk Maxwell's paper was read to the Royal Society in December 1864. Heinrich Hertz experimentally confirmed the existence of radio waves in 1887, nine years after Maxwell died of cancer at 48. Richard Feynman called Maxwell's equations "the most significant event of the 19th century" — a bold statement given the century's competition.

events.title: X-Rays Discovered
events.blurb: While experimenting with cathode ray tubes in a darkened laboratory, a German physicist noticed that a fluorescent screen across the room glowed even though it was shielded from the tube's visible light. The mysterious new rays penetrated cardboard, wood, and flesh, but were blocked by dense metal. Within weeks he had produced the first medical radiograph, showing the bones of his wife's hand.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1895 — Wilhelm Röntgen kept the discovery secret for seven weeks, repeating every experiment before telling anyone. He named the rays "X" because he didn't know what they were. He won the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 and donated the prize money to his university.

events.title: Radioactivity Discovered
events.blurb: A French physicist studying uranium salts placed a wrapped photographic plate in a drawer alongside a uranium sample during several cloudy days, expecting to run a sunlight experiment later. When he developed the plate anyway, he found a sharp image — proving the uranium was spontaneously emitting invisible radiation with no external energy source, a phenomenon no existing theory could explain.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1896 — Henri Becquerel announced to the Academy of Sciences that the image was "very distinct." The discovery was accidental: bad weather cancelled his planned sunlight experiment. He initially thought it was a variant of X-rays; it took the Curies to show radioactivity was a property of the atom itself.

events.title: General Relativity Confirmed by Eclipse
events.blurb: Two British expeditions sent to observe a total solar eclipse measured the positions of stars near the Sun's edge and found their apparent positions had shifted by an amount predicted by a new theory of gravitation — confirming that massive objects warp the fabric of space itself. The results overturned the classical picture of gravity as a force acting at a distance and made the paper's author internationally famous overnight.
events.revealBlurb: November 6, 1919 — Arthur Eddington announced the results to a packed joint meeting of the Royal Society and Royal Astronomical Society in London. The Times headline read "Revolution in Science." Some later scholars questioned the data quality, but multiple subsequent eclipses fully confirmed the result.

events.title: Seneca Falls Convention
events.blurb: Three hundred people, a third of them men, gathered for two days at a Methodist chapel in upstate New York for the first women's rights convention held in the United States. Participants approved a "Declaration of Sentiments" modelled on the Declaration of Independence, demanding legal equality in marriage, property, education, employment, and the franchise. Only one resolution — women's suffrage — passed by a narrow vote.
events.revealBlurb: July 19-20, 1848 — Seneca Falls, NY. Lead organizers Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott. Only one signer, 19-year-old Charlotte Woodward, lived to vote in a federal election 72 years later. She was 91 and bed-ridden on Election Day 1920 and could not make it to the polls.

events.title: Susan B. Anthony Votes
events.blurb: A 52-year-old suffragist and 14 other women presented themselves at a polling place in their upstate New York city and demanded to register to vote, citing the language of the recently ratified 14th Amendment. Three inspectors, after consulting the U.S. constitution, let them register. On election day four days later she voted; she was arrested two weeks after that. Her trial, the following year, denied her the right to testify in her own defense.
events.revealBlurb: November 5, 1872 — Rochester, NY. Judge Ward Hunt fined her $100; she refused ever to pay. The U.S. has since put her face on a coin that was widely disliked and quickly withdrawn (the 1979 dollar).

events.title: Jeannette Rankin Elected to Congress
events.blurb: A 36-year-old social worker and suffrage organizer from a western U.S. state was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives, becoming the first woman to hold federal office in the country. She took office four years before women nationally could vote. She would vote against entering both world wars — the only member of Congress to do so twice.
events.revealBlurb: November 7, 1916 — Montana had given women the state vote in 1914. Rankin's 1941 "no" vote on the declaration of war against Japan made her a pariah; she had to be escorted to her office by the Capitol police. "As a woman I can't go to war," she said, "and I refuse to send anyone else."

events.title: 19th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Seven decades after a convention in upstate New York had narrowly resolved that women ought to vote, a Tennessee state legislator cast the deciding vote for his state's ratification — after reading a telegram from his mother urging him to do so. Women across the United States gained the national vote in time for the November presidential election, in which 8 million new voters participated.
events.revealBlurb: August 18, 1920 — the deciding vote was cast by Harry T. Burn, age 24. His mother's letter read: "Hurrah, and vote for suffrage. Don't keep them in doubt." The amendment was certified on August 26, now Women's Equality Day.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Cortés Reaches Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Spanish conquistador, in defiance of orders from the governor of Cuba who had tried to recall him, entered the causeway-linked lakeside capital of the Aztec Triple Alliance — a city of perhaps 200,000 people, one of the largest in the world, built on an island in a high-altitude lake. The Aztec emperor met him with courtesy, gifts, and quiet suspicion. Within two years the emperor would be dead and the city in ruins.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1519 — Hernán Cortés meets Moctezuma II in Tenochtitlán (modern Mexico City). The Spanish force was about 500 strong, augmented by thousands of Tlaxcalan allies who hated the Aztecs. Cortés had burned his own ships on the coast to prevent desertion.

events.title: First Circumnavigation Complete
events.blurb: The last seaworthy ship of a Spanish expedition that had set out three years earlier with five vessels dropped anchor in the Guadalquivir River in Spain — the first ship ever to return to its port of departure after sailing completely around the world. Of the 270 men who had departed, 18 returned alive. Its captain, though no longer the expedition's original commander — who had been killed in the Philippines — had personally sailed the ship the entire way home.
events.revealBlurb: September 6, 1522 — Juan Sebastián Elcano aboard the Victoria. The voyage proved the earth was circumnavigable, and also forced the first adjustment of the ship's log by a day (a precursor to the concept of the International Date Line). Elcano himself died at sea in 1526, three ships into another expedition.

events.title: Dissolution of Monasteries Begins
events.blurb: Two years after the English king's break with Rome, an Act of Parliament authorized the seizure of smaller English monasteries — those with annual revenues under £200 — along with their lands, buildings, and moveable wealth. A second Act four years later did the same for the larger houses. Within four years, every monastic institution in the kingdom was gone; their lands were sold to loyalists at bargain prices, creating a new class of Tudor gentry.
events.revealBlurb: March 1536 — First Suppression Act under Henry VIII, advised by Thomas Cromwell. Roughly 800 religious houses were closed; their lands made up about a quarter of England's entire land area. Many gorgeous medieval abbeys — Tintern, Fountains, Glastonbury — survive today as evocative ruins.

events.title: Shakespeare's First Folio
events.blurb: Seven years after the Stratford-born playwright's death, two of his fellow actors compiled and published a folio edition of 36 of his plays — 18 of which had never been printed before. Without the volume, half the plays, including Macbeth, Julius Caesar, and The Tempest, would have been lost. 750 copies were printed; 235 are known to survive today, fetching tens of millions at auction.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1623 — compiled by John Heminges and Henry Condell. It was sold for £1 — roughly £200 today. A recently discovered copy was unmasked at a Scottish library in 2016. The folio standardized the canonical text of most of the plays.

events.title: Truman Doctrine
events.blurb: Addressing a joint session of Congress, a U.S. president requested $400 million in aid for Greece and Turkey and announced a sweeping new foreign policy: the United States would support "free peoples" resisting armed minorities or outside pressures. The speech committed America to global containment of communism.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1947 — Harry Truman needed just 18 minutes. Behind the rhetoric: Britain, bankrupted by war, had quietly told Washington it could no longer prop up the Greek government. America stepped into the imperial vacuum.

events.title: Korean War Begins
events.blurb: In the pre-dawn darkness, roughly 75,000 soldiers of a northern peninsular state poured south across the 38th parallel, overwhelming border defenses and driving south within days. The United Nations Security Council, with the Soviet representative boycotting, voted to intervene — the first shooting war between major powers since 1945.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1950 — Kim Il-sung's forces crossed the parallel. The USSR was boycotting the UN over China's representation, which is why the Soviet veto didn't stop intervention. MacArthur's Inchon landing three months later turned the war.

events.title: "Tear Down This Wall" Speech
events.blurb: Speaking in front of the Brandenburg Gate in a divided German city, a U.S. president issued a direct public challenge to the Soviet leader: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!" The State Department had tried to cut the line from the draft four times, considering it inflammatory. The president insisted. Twenty-eight months later, the wall fell.
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1987 — Reagan in West Berlin. The phrase went mostly unremarked at the time; American newspapers buried it. Its posthumous fame owes more to the actual wall's 1989 collapse than to anything it said in the moment.

events.title: Berlin Wall Falls
events.blurb: An East German government spokesman announced at a press conference that citizens could cross the border immediately, triggering jubilant crowds who arrived at checkpoints and began dismantling the 155-kilometre concrete barrier with hammers and their bare hands. More than two million East Germans crossed into West Berlin during the following weekend alone.

events.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
events.blurb: An East German spokesman, reading hastily from a note and misunderstanding its contents, announced at a televised press conference that new travel rules would take effect "immediately." Within hours, tens of thousands of jubilant East Berliners massed at the crossings. Confused border guards, receiving no clear orders, simply let them through. People scrambled onto the concrete barrier with hammers.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 1989 — the spokesman was Günter Schabowski, who had skimmed the briefing note just before the press conference. Asked when the rules took effect, he shrugged: "As far as I know — immediately." The wall, built in a single night 28 years earlier, came down in a single night too.

events.title: UNIVAC Predicts Election
events.blurb: A televised presidential election broadcast featured, as a novelty, a commercial digital computer that had been sold to the Census Bureau six months earlier. Fed early returns by its operators, the machine predicted an Eisenhower landslide hours before conventional forecasters were willing to call the race. CBS' broadcasters initially didn't trust it and understated its projection on-air. The machine was right.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 1952 — UNIVAC I, on CBS. The machine predicted 438 electoral votes for Eisenhower; the actual result was 442. After the election, CBS' on-air introducer Charles Collingwood admitted they had held back UNIVAC's early call for fear it would look ridiculous.

events.title: Microsoft Founded
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore and his 22-year-old friend, working out of a cheap room in an Albuquerque motel, formally established a partnership to develop software for microcomputers. Their first product had been a BASIC interpreter for the Altair 8800, licensed to the kit's manufacturer. The contract paid royalties per machine sold. Within seven years they would own the personal-computer operating system industry.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1975 — Bill Gates and Paul Allen. Originally "Micro-Soft." They moved to the Seattle suburb of Bellevue in 1979 and to Redmond in 1986. Allen left the company in 1983 after being diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma; he recovered, founded other businesses, died in 2018.

events.title: Sony Walkman Released
events.blurb: A Japanese electronics company released a portable personal cassette player, weighing 390 grams, with headphones instead of a speaker. It had no record function — unusual for a cassette player — and its CEO personally insisted on this as a way of encouraging private, solitary music consumption. The device created an entirely new product category and pulled portable listening out of the car radio and boombox and into the individual's pocket for the next quarter-century.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 1979 — Sony TPS-L2. Co-founder Masaru Ibuka had wanted something compact to enjoy opera on long flights. The original name in Japan was "Walkman"; in the US, "Soundabout"; in the UK, "Stowaway." "Walkman" eventually won out globally.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: Apple M1 Chip Released
events.blurb: A California computer company released the first Mac laptops powered by a chip it had designed in-house, based on the ARM instruction set. The M1 provided substantially better performance per watt than the Intel chips Apple had shipped in Macs for 15 years. Reviews were rapturous; the company would completely abandon Intel chips across its laptop and desktop lines within two years. The industry's Intel-based personal-computer architecture lost a long-standing stranglehold.
events.revealBlurb: November 10, 2020 — Apple M1. The chip integrated CPU, GPU, and memory into a single package. It was the first mainstream consumer computer to use ARM rather than x86 since the 1990s. The Mac Pro completed the Intel-to-Apple Silicon transition in 2023.

events.title: Michael Jackson Dies
events.blurb: A 50-year-old American singer widely regarded as the most successful pop star of his generation died of cardiac arrest at his rented Los Angeles home while preparing for a 50-concert comeback tour in London. His personal physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter for administering propofol, a surgical anesthetic, to help him sleep. His death prompted an outpouring of grief that crashed major websites and sold over 35 million of his records in the following six months.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 2009 — Michael Jackson. His physician, Conrad Murray, was sentenced to 4 years and served 2. His public memorial on July 7 drew 31 million U.S. TV viewers. The "This Is It" concert film, compiled from rehearsal footage, grossed $261 million posthumously.

events.title: Gangnam Style Goes Viral
events.blurb: A music video by a 34-year-old South Korean rapper was uploaded to YouTube, featuring a catchy synth-pop track, exaggerated dance moves, and satirical shots of an upscale Seoul district. Within three months the video had 300 million views, passing Justin Bieber's "Baby" as the most-viewed in YouTube history. Within five, it crossed one billion. The horse-riding dance broke through into American late-night comedy, political campaigns, and every wedding reception in the world.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 2012 — PSY (Park Jae-sang). It held the most-viewed YouTube video title until it was surpassed by "See You Again" in 2017 and then "Despacito." The video's 2014 view count literally broke YouTube's 32-bit counter, requiring an engineering upgrade to 64 bits.

events.title: Kim Kardashian "Breaks the Internet"
events.blurb: A 34-year-old reality TV star and entrepreneur appeared on the cover of a magazine nude, balancing a champagne glass on her bared posterior, with a headline directly daring the internet to be broken by it. The cover image was shared widely enough that the magazine's website crashed for short periods. The photograph — shot by a French photographer who had staged similar images four decades earlier — launched weeks of commentary about sexuality, race, body image, and the limits of viral marketing.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 2014 — Kim Kardashian on Paper magazine. Photographer Jean-Paul Goude had shot nearly identical images with other models in the 1970s and 80s, drawing accusations that he specifically emphasized and sexualized Black bodies. The cover did, in fact, briefly break the magazine's website.

events.title: "The Dress" Goes Viral
events.blurb: A 21-year-old Scottish woman posted a photograph of a dress on her Tumblr account asking for help settling a family argument — was it black and blue, or white and gold? The photo went viral overnight. Approximately 40 percent of viewers saw it as white and gold; 50 percent as black and blue. Vision scientists spent months examining why. The actual dress, in real life, was black and blue. The phenomenon became a landmark case study in how individual visual perception varies based on assumptions about ambient lighting.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2015 — Cecilia Bleasdale's photograph, posted by Caitlin McNeill. Roman Originals, who made the dress, saw a 560 percent spike in sales. Neuroscientists published papers on it for years. It revived serious research into color constancy and top-down visual processing.

events.title: Stranger Things Premieres
events.blurb: A supernatural drama set in a small Indiana town in 1983 premiered on Netflix, combining Spielbergian child adventure, Stephen King atmospheric horror, and 80s-movie production design with a pitch-perfect synth-wave score. The 8-episode first season was Netflix's first genuine original-production cultural sensation and proved that the streaming service could create prestige-TV hits without a traditional network. The cast of unknown child actors became overnight celebrities.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 2016 — Netflix; created by the Duffer Brothers. Cast included Winona Ryder, David Harbour, Millie Bobby Brown, Finn Wolfhard, Noah Schnapp. The 2022 season 4 episode "Running Up That Hill" pushed Kate Bush's 1985 single to #1 in the UK, 37 years after its original release.

events.title: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake Premieres
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Russian composer's first full-length ballet score premiered at a grand theatre in the Russian capital, paired with choreography that was widely thought incompetent and dancing that was widely thought under-rehearsed. Critics focused their complaints on the music, which they found too "symphonic" for dancing. Only after the composer's death, in a restaged 1895 version with new choreography, did the ballet become a classic.
events.revealBlurb: March 4, 1877 — Pyotr Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake at the Bolshoi, Moscow (Old Style February 20). The 1895 St. Petersburg revival with Petipa/Ivanov choreography is the version most companies perform today. The tragic black-swan finale was a 1950s restoration.

events.title: Louis Armstrong's Hot Fives
events.blurb: A 24-year-old cornetist who had grown up in the poorest section of New Orleans walked into a Chicago studio for the first session with a small band of his own. Over the next three years, the "Hot Five" and "Hot Seven" sessions would reshape popular music. His vocal improvisation on "Heebie Jeebies" — a chorus of nonsense syllables when he claimed to drop his lyric sheet — launched scat singing. His trumpet solos made the individual improvisation the heart of jazz.
events.revealBlurb: November 12, 1925 — Louis Armstrong at OKeh Records, Chicago. The "Heebie Jeebies" vocal made him a national figure. He would become the first African-American to host a nationally sponsored radio show.

events.title: Led Zeppelin IV Released
events.blurb: A British rock band released their fourth album with no title, no text, and no band name anywhere on the cover — just a painting of an old man with a bundle of firewood on his back. The album contained eight tracks, including an eight-minute multi-part track that would become the most-played song on American FM radio for a decade. Critics were lukewarm; listeners bought 37 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1971 — Led Zeppelin IV, featuring "Stairway to Heaven." The band was so angered by critical reception of the previous album that they refused to identify themselves on this one. The old man on the cover was a real picture bought from an antique shop in Reading.

events.title: Hip-Hop Born in the Bronx
events.blurb: An 18-year-old Jamaican-born DJ, using two turntables to extend the instrumental breaks of funk and soul records, played his younger sister's back-to-school party in the rec room of a public housing building in the South Bronx. His technique of looping drum breaks became the foundation of hip-hop. The party went so well that he began DJ-ing at local parks and block parties; rappers (then called MCs) began performing over his sets. A new culture was born.
events.revealBlurb: August 11, 1973 — DJ Kool Herc (Clive Campbell) at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, the Bronx. The address is now a national historic site. Herc's "merry-go-round" technique of using two copies of the same record to loop the break is still the foundation of every hip-hop DJ set.

events.title: Thriller Released
events.blurb: A 24-year-old singer released his sixth studio album, a collection of nine tracks deliberately designed so every one could be a single. The 14-minute title track's horror-film music video, featuring choreographed zombie dancing, premiered the following December on a cable channel that had until recently been reluctant to play Black artists. The album became, and remains, the best-selling album of all time.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 1982 — Michael Jackson, produced by Quincy Jones. It has sold over 70 million copies worldwide. The moonwalk, which Jackson debuted performing "Billie Jean" at Motown's 25th-anniversary TV special 3.5 months after release, was not actually his invention.

events.title: Iliad and Odyssey Composed
events.blurb: Oral-tradition epic poems about a mythic ten-year siege of a city in western Anatolia and the homecoming of a Greek king after it, composed or consolidated by a blind Ionian bard — or a school of bards working in his name — were set to writing for the first time, probably by scribes who took them down from live recitation. They would become the foundation texts of Greek literature, education, and religion.
events.revealBlurb: c. 750 BCE — traditionally ascribed to Homer. The "Homeric question" — whether one poet, many poets, or an oral tradition produced them — is still unresolved. The war they describe may reflect faint memory of Bronze Age conflicts around the archaeological site of Troy.

events.title: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
events.blurb: An English civil servant in his mid-fifties died leaving unfinished a collection of stories told by pilgrims riding from Southwark to a Kentish cathedral shrine. Written in Middle English rather than French or Latin, the work demonstrated the poetic range of the English vernacular across a social spectrum — knights, millers, cooks, pardoners, the famously bawdy Wife of Bath. Only 24 of a planned 120 tales were ever completed.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1400 — Geoffrey Chaucer. He is often called the father of English literature. Roughly 80 manuscripts survive; the earliest complete ones date from the 1410s. The Wife of Bath's Tale became an early feminist touchstone.

events.title: War and Peace Published
events.blurb: A 41-year-old Russian aristocrat completed the last serial installment of a vast historical novel following five aristocratic families through Russia's Napoleonic Wars. The finished work ran over 1,200 pages and combined personal drama, military history, and a 200-page essay on the philosophy of history tacked onto the end. The author rewrote the opening sentence at least seven times.
events.revealBlurb: 1869 — Leo Tolstoy. It was serialized in the journal Russky Vestnik between 1865 and 1869. Tolstoy later disowned most of his fiction on religious grounds and decades later attempted to destroy his own estate's copyright to prevent his heirs from profiting.

events.title: Treasure Island Published
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish writer, suffering severe pulmonary illness and convalescing in the Scottish Highlands, sketched a treasure map with his 12-year-old stepson on a rainy afternoon and began improvising a story for the boy. The serialized pirate adventure novel that grew from the map — featuring a peg-legged cook, a squawking parrot, a buried fortune, and a black spot — essentially defined the iconography of piracy for the next century and a half.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 1883 — Robert Louis Stevenson. Initially serialized in the magazine Young Folks in 1881 as "The Sea Cook." The phrase "Shiver me timbers!" does not appear in the book but was popularized by its Long John Silver.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: "Who Shot J.R.?" Revealed
events.blurb: An estimated 83 million American viewers — 76 percent of all active television sets at the time — tuned in to a prime-time U.S. soap opera to learn who had fired the cliffhanger-ending shot that had kept the nation guessing for eight months. At the time it was the most-watched single program in television history. Souvenir T-shirts, novelty songs, and betting pools had all sprouted during the summer hiatus between seasons.
events.revealBlurb: November 21, 1980 — Dallas, episode "Who Done It." The shooter was Kristin Shepard, played by Mary Crosby. J.R. Ewing survived. The "Who Shot J.R.?" plot is considered a pioneer of the season-ending cliffhanger in prime-time television.

events.title: Prince Charles Marries Diana
events.blurb: The heir to the British throne, 32, married a 20-year-old shy nursery-school assistant at a grand ceremony at a London cathedral. The televised wedding drew 750 million viewers worldwide and unfolded like a fairytale: horse-drawn carriages, a 25-foot train on the bride's silk ivory dress, a balcony kiss at a royal palace afterward. The marriage itself would be miserable; the couple separated in 1992 and divorced in 1996. Both remarried others, and the bride died in a Paris car crash in 1997.
events.revealBlurb: July 29, 1981 — Charles, Prince of Wales and Lady Diana Spencer at St. Paul's Cathedral. Diana tripped on her father's name during the vows ("Philip Charles Arthur George" instead of "Charles Philip..."). Charles, now King Charles III, succeeded his mother Elizabeth II in September 2022.

events.title: Apple's "1984" Super Bowl Ad
events.blurb: A 60-second commercial produced by a British director for a California computer company aired during the third quarter of the Super Bowl. The ad showed a dystopian audience of grey workers watching a Big-Brother-like speaker on a vast screen; an athletic woman in running clothes smashed the screen with a hammer. The product was the Macintosh computer. Apple's board had voted to kill the ad; the CEO insisted it air. It aired once.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1984 — directed by Ridley Scott. The ad ran nationally only that one time; it has since been shown as a promotion or film-clip thousands of times. Macintosh sales in its first 100 days exceeded expectations. The "1984" ad is still considered one of the greatest commercials ever made.

events.title: Milli Vanilli Grammy Stripped
events.blurb: The Recording Academy revoked a Grammy award given to a German-based pop duo nine months earlier after the duo's producer, fired in a dispute, revealed publicly that the duo had not actually sung on their multi-platinum album — other studio vocalists had. The two dreadlocked frontmen had been, in effect, models who lip-synced. The scandal ended their careers; the Recording Academy has not revoked a Grammy for any reason since.
events.revealBlurb: November 19, 1990 — Milli Vanilli (Rob Pilatus and Fab Morvan) stripped of their 1989 Best New Artist Grammy. Rob Pilatus was found dead in 1998 at 32 of an accidental overdose. Fab Morvan has continued to perform. The actual vocalists included Charles Shaw, John Davis, and Brad Howell.

events.title: Nevermind Released
events.blurb: A three-piece rock band from Aberdeen, Washington released their second album featuring a swimming infant reaching for a dollar bill on a fishhook. Within three months it had displaced a reigning pop star's record from the top of the Billboard 200, and its lead single's music video received more plays on music television than any previous video.

events.title: Stonehenge Completed
events.blurb: Over the course of a millennium, Neolithic builders on a chalk plain in southern England erected a circular arrangement of massive standing stones — some weighing 25 tonnes, dragged from quarries over 250 kilometres away — fitted together with mortise-and-tenon joints as if they were timber. The monument aligns with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. Its precise purpose — ritual, astronomical, funerary — has been debated for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2000 BCE — main sarsen-circle completion on Salisbury Plain. The smaller "bluestones," of volcanic rock, came from the Preseli Hills in Wales. Construction had begun about 5,000 years ago in earthen-bank form. The monument predates the druids by 2,000 years, despite the misattribution.

events.title: Versailles Hall of Mirrors Completed
events.blurb: A French king's chief architect and royal painter completed the centerpiece of a vastly enlarged royal palace on the edge of Paris — a 73-metre-long gallery of 578 mirror panels on one side, facing 17 tall windows overlooking the palace gardens on the other, with a vaulted ceiling painted with 30 scenes of the king's military triumphs. Mirrors were at the time so expensive that a single pane could cost as much as a small estate; the gallery was a showcase of French glassmaking independence from Venice.
events.revealBlurb: 1684 — Jules Hardouin-Mansart (architect) and Charles Le Brun (painter) for Louis XIV. The Treaty of Versailles ending WWI was signed in the room on June 28, 1919 — a deliberate German humiliation in the same space where German unification had been proclaimed in 1871.

events.title: St. Paul's Cathedral Completed
events.blurb: After 35 years of construction replacing a medieval cathedral destroyed in the Great Fire of London, a 68-year-old English architect watched his son install the final piece of his new cathedral's lantern atop its dome — the first cathedral anywhere in the world to have been entirely designed, built, and completed by a single architect within his own lifetime. The triple-domed design, inspired by St. Peter's in Rome, rose 111 metres above the City of London.
events.revealBlurb: 1710 — Sir Christopher Wren. He also designed 52 other London churches after the Great Fire of 1666. He was buried in the cathedral's crypt when he died in 1723 at 90; his memorial reads "Si monumentum requiris, circumspice" — if you seek his monument, look around you.

events.title: Suez Canal Opens
events.blurb: The French-designed 193-kilometre sea-level canal linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea — dug largely by corvée (unpaid forced) Egyptian labour over ten years with massive loss of life — opened to international traffic. A procession of 68 ships led by a French imperial yacht sailed from Port Said to the Red Sea over four days. The canal cut the sea route from London to Bombay by about 7,200 kilometres and shifted the geography of global trade.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1869 — designer Ferdinand de Lesseps. Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, commissioned by Khedive Ismail for the opening, arrived too late and premiered in 1871. The canal was nationalized by Egypt in 1956, triggering the Suez Crisis.

events.title: Empire State Building Opens
events.blurb: A 381-metre, 102-story skyscraper opened in Manhattan, having been designed in two weeks and constructed in just 410 days — often at a rate of 4.5 stories per week. It displaced the Chrysler Building as the tallest building in the world and held that title for 41 years. The Great Depression left it mostly empty for its first decade; New Yorkers nicknamed it the "Empty State Building." It entered profit in 1950.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1931 — architect William F. Lamb (Shreve, Lamb and Harmon). The B-25 bomber that crashed into the 79th floor in heavy fog on July 28, 1945 killed 14 people but damaged the structure only moderately. King Kong famously climbed it in the 1933 film.

events.title: Drake Strikes Oil
events.blurb: A former railroad conductor, working on behalf of a small Pennsylvania oil-extraction company, struck oil at a depth of 21 metres while drilling a well using salt-drilling techniques borrowed from Chinese craftsmen. The well produced about 25 barrels a day — at the time, world-altering. Within two years, western Pennsylvania had hundreds of wells; within twenty, American oil companies were exporting kerosene around the world; within fifty, petroleum had overtaken coal as the premier industrial fuel.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1859 — Edwin Drake at Titusville, Pennsylvania. Drake himself died poor; he had failed to patent his drilling-pipe innovations. John D. Rockefeller entered the Cleveland refining business five years later and, with Standard Oil, came to dominate the industry within a decade.

events.title: Edison Invents Phonograph
events.blurb: A 30-year-old American inventor shouted the first verse of "Mary Had a Little Lamb" into the horn of a machine he had built at his New Jersey laboratory, then cranked a handle to make the machine play his words back to him. Recording sound — not just transmitting it instantaneously as the telephone did — had never been done before. The device, a tinfoil-cylinder phonograph, would be followed by commercial wax-cylinder versions by the end of the decade.
events.revealBlurb: November 21, 1877 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. The original tinfoil phonograph could replay a recording only a few times before the foil wore out. The machine astonished audiences when Edison demonstrated it at the Scientific American office a week later.

events.title: Brooklyn Bridge Opens
events.blurb: The longest suspension bridge in the world — 486 metres between its Gothic granite towers — opened to foot and carriage traffic linking Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Its construction had taken 14 years and cost 27 lives. The chief engineer had been paralyzed by decompression sickness while supervising caisson work; his wife Emily had effectively managed the final decade of the project from notes dictated in his sickroom.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1883 — designed by John A. Roebling (who died from a dockside accident early in construction). His son Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease and was bedridden; daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling led onsite engineering management. She was the first person to cross the completed bridge, in a carriage carrying a rooster.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Ford Model T Goes on Sale
events.blurb: An American automaker released a new car designed to be cheap, simple to drive, and reliable on the rutted rural roads of the era. It sold for $850 — about half the price of the cheapest competitor. Over 19 years of production, the company would build 15 million of them, mostly painted black because that paint dried fastest. At peak production, a completed Model T rolled off the line every 24 seconds.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1908 — Ford Motor Company. The 1913-1914 introduction of the moving assembly line cut the Model T's price to $490. Henry Ford doubled the minimum wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day in January 1914, partly to cut turnover caused by the line's brutal monotony.

events.title: Columbus Makes Landfall
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator commanding three vessels landed on an island in the present-day Bahamas after 70 days at sea, believing he had reached islands off the coast of Asia. He planted a royal standard, claimed the land in the name of the Spanish Crown, and named the island San Salvador — its indigenous inhabitants called it Guanahani.

events.title: Vasco da Gama Reaches India
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Portuguese captain, after a 10-month voyage south around the southern tip of Africa and up its eastern coast, dropped anchor at a spice port on the Malabar coast of India. He had sailed further than any previous European expedition. The local ruler was unimpressed by the trinkets he offered as tribute, but the sea route to Asian spices — breaking the Venetian and Arab overland monopoly — was now open.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1498 — Vasco da Gama at Calicut (Kozhikode), India. His expedition had left Lisbon with 170 men; 54 returned alive. He would make two more voyages and die in India in 1524 as the country's viceroy.

events.title: Elizabeth I Accession
events.blurb: A 25-year-old unmarried princess, the daughter of a beheaded second queen who had once been declared a bastard, became Queen of England on the death of her half-sister. She had survived imprisonment and political marginalization under her sister's Catholic restoration. Her 44-year reign would see the English settlement of Ireland, the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the flowering of Shakespeare, and the establishment of a Protestant national church still in existence.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1558 — Elizabeth I Tudor succeeds Mary I. She reportedly received the news sitting under an oak tree at Hatfield House. She never married, styled herself the "Virgin Queen," and died at 69. The state of Virginia — briefly colonized under her — is named for her.

events.title: Edict of Nantes
events.blurb: The first Bourbon king of France, a former Protestant who had converted to Catholicism to secure his crown ("Paris is worth a Mass"), issued an edict guaranteeing Protestant Huguenots freedom of worship in specific towns, civil equality, and the right to maintain their own fortified places. The compromise ended 36 years of Wars of Religion and was the most expansive grant of religious toleration any European state had yet made. His grandson would revoke it 87 years later.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1598 — Henry IV of France. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, triggering a Protestant exodus of perhaps 400,000 skilled workers. Henry IV himself was assassinated by a Catholic fanatic in 1610.

events.title: Mayflower Compact Signed
events.blurb: 41 male passengers of a merchant ship that had landed at the wrong spot on the Massachusetts coast — they had intended the Hudson River — signed a short agreement on the ship to govern themselves by the will of the majority until permanent civil authority could be established. The document was pragmatic, not ideological, but became a foundational text of American self-government. The Pilgrims who signed it were fleeing religious persecution in England via the Netherlands.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 1620 (Old Style) / November 21, 1620 (New Style) — aboard the Mayflower, Cape Cod. Half the colony's 102 passengers died of scurvy and starvation the first winter. The autumn 1621 harvest feast with the Wampanoag is the ancestor of the American Thanksgiving.

events.title: Space Invaders Hits Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: An alien formation that descended one row lower every time a column was destroyed — a quirk of the hardware clock — accidentally created the defining tension mechanic of arcade games. The game was so popular in Japan that bars converted into dedicated parlours.
events.revealBlurb: July 1978 — Taito released Space Invaders in Japan. The Atari 2600 home port in 1980 quadrupled console sales that year. The "yen coin shortage" is an urban legend — numismatists have found no evidence in mint records.

events.title: Asteroids Released by Atari
events.blurb: Drawing lines on a vector monitor to simulate drifting through space debris sounds modest. The game that resulted became Atari's best-selling arcade cabinet of all time, pulling in an estimated 10 million quarters per day at its peak. Demand was so extreme that Atari temporarily halted production of other games and shipped Asteroids units inside Lunar Lander cabinets just to get them out the door faster.
events.revealBlurb: November 1979 — Atari released Asteroids in North American arcades. It sold over 70,000 cabinets. The game's high score table was the first widely adopted public performance metric in gaming — and the first subject of documented high-score fraud.

events.title: Pac-Man Debuts in Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: A yellow circle eating dots and fleeing ghosts through a maze seemed like a peculiar bet in an era dominated by shoot-'em-ups. It became the highest-grossing arcade game ever made, the first video game character to achieve mass-market celebrity, and the template for an entirely new genre. Its creator wanted a game that women would actually want to play.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1980 — Namco's Puck-Man (renamed Pac-Man for Western markets to prevent vandalism) went on location test in Shibuya, Tokyo. By 1982 an estimated 30 billion quarters had been inserted into Pac-Man machines worldwide.

events.title: The Sims Released
events.blurb: A game in which you build a house and manage the life of a simulated person — feeding them, making them use the bathroom, watching them catch fire if left unattended too long — became the best-selling PC game of the year, and then 2001, and then the best-selling PC game of all time. More than half its players were women, permanently disproving every assumption the games industry held about its audience.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2000 — Maxis and EA released The Sims for Windows. It sold 1.77 million copies in North America in its first year. The Sims overtook Myst to become the best-selling PC game ever in 2002. The franchise has sold over 70 million copies.

events.title: World of Warcraft Launches
events.blurb: An online game that charged a monthly subscription fee on top of a $50 box price acquired half a million players in its first week and 12 million at its peak — more than the population of several European nations. It swallowed years of people's lives, birthed the term "raiding," generated academic papers about its simulated epidemics, and made "massively multiplayer" a standard genre.
events.revealBlurb: November 23, 2004 — World of Warcraft launched in North America, Australia, and New Zealand. In 2020, researchers cited WoW's 2005 "Corrupted Blood" plague — an accidental in-game epidemic — as a realistic model for studying pandemic behaviour. Lifetime revenue exceeded $9 billion.

events.title: Battle of New Orleans
events.blurb: General Andrew Jackson's patchwork army of Tennessee frontiersmen, Louisiana militia, free Black soldiers, Choctaw warriors, and pirates under Jean Lafitte decisively routed an 8,000-strong British force attempting to seize New Orleans, killing or wounding roughly 2,000 redcoats while suffering fewer than 70 American casualties. The lopsided victory made Jackson a national hero and propelled him to the presidency.
events.revealBlurb: January 8, 1815 — Chalmette, Louisiana. The Treaty of Ghent ending the War of 1812 had been signed 15 days earlier — news hadn't arrived. The battle had zero effect on the war's official outcome but enormous effect on American mythology and Jackson's political career.

events.title: Caning of Senator Charles Sumner
events.blurb: Representative Preston Brooks of South Carolina strode onto the Senate floor and beat Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts unconscious with a metal-topped gutta-percha cane, inflicting such severe head injuries that Sumner could not return to his seat for over three years. The assault came two days after Sumner delivered a blistering antislavery speech mocking Brooks's cousin; Massachusetts left Sumner's empty desk on display as a rebuke.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1856 — U.S. Senate chamber. Brooks resigned, was immediately re-elected by South Carolina, and received commemorative canes inscribed "Hit Him Again." Sumner's empty desk served as visible propaganda for the antislavery cause for three years. The incident convinced many Northerners that slavery corrupted men beyond reason.

events.title: Gettysburg Address Delivered
events.blurb: At the dedication of a military cemetery on the grounds of the bloodiest battle of the war, Abraham Lincoln delivered a 272-word speech that redefined the purpose of the conflict — not merely preserving the Union, but completing the "unfinished work" of the Declaration of Independence by ensuring that a government of the people would not perish. Lincoln spoke for less than two minutes; the main orator that day delivered a two-hour speech that nobody remembers.
events.revealBlurb: November 19, 1863 — Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. The battle four months earlier killed or wounded more than 50,000 men over three days. Edward Everett — the two-hour orator — wrote Lincoln privately: "I should be glad if I could flatter myself that I came as near to the central idea of the occasion, in two hours, as you did in two minutes."

events.title: Teapot Dome: Senate Investigation Opens
events.blurb: The Senate launched its first formal investigation into the Teapot Dome oil fields that autumn, following revelations that Interior Secretary Albert Fall had secretly leased federal naval petroleum reserves in Wyoming and California to private oil companies in exchange for personal cash loans and gifts totaling roughly $400,000. Fall would become the first U.S. Cabinet member ever convicted of a crime committed while in office.
events.revealBlurb: October 1923 — Washington, D.C. The oil companies that paid the bribes — Sinclair Oil and Pan American Petroleum — were acquitted at trial; only the man who took the bribes was convicted. President Harding died of a heart attack in August 1923, before the scandal fully broke.

events.title: President Kennedy Assassinated in Dallas
events.blurb: At approximately 12:30 pm that day, President John F. Kennedy was shot in the head while riding in an open motorcade through Dealey Plaza in Dallas, Texas, and was pronounced dead at Parkland Memorial Hospital at 1:00 pm. Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested that afternoon; two days later, Oswald was shot and killed on live national television by nightclub owner Jack Ruby before he could stand trial.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1963 — Dallas, Texas. Lyndon Johnson was sworn in as president on Air Force One, with a blood-spattered Jacqueline Kennedy standing beside him. The Warren Commission concluded Oswald acted alone; roughly 60% of Americans have never believed it.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.blurb: The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the sixteen-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna — a boy whose mocking nickname meant "Little Augustus" — and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, informing the eastern emperor that the west no longer needed a separate ruler. Odoacer spared Romulus's life, finding him too young and too minor to bother executing, and exiled him to a villa in Campania on a pension.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 476 CE. The last western emperor's name combined the city's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony Roman writers noticed immediately. Contemporaries did not regard this moment as "the fall of Rome"; that framing came centuries later. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued for another 977 years.

events.title: Battle of Tours
events.blurb: A Frankish mayor of the palace led an infantry army into a defensive wall of shields against a much larger Umayyad cavalry force that had been raiding deep into western Europe. The battle's outcome stopped the northward expansion of the Islamic caliphate into the Frankish heartland and established the Carolingian dynasty as the dominant power of the region.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 732 — Charles Martel ("Charles the Hammer") in central France. His grandson Charlemagne would be crowned emperor 68 years later. Edward Gibbon later wrote that without the victory, "the interpretation of the Koran would now be taught in the schools of Oxford."

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: University of Bologna Founded
events.blurb: A self-organized guild of foreign students in a northern Italian city hired local scholars to lecture them on civil and canon law, and the informal arrangement crystallized into something new: a chartered community with legal privileges, standardized exams, and a governing rector elected by the students themselves. It is considered the oldest continuously operating university in the Western world.
events.revealBlurb: 1088 — date traditionally given, though the institution evolved over decades. The students were mostly the sons of wealthy families across Europe; they often hired the professors directly and fined them for being late to class. Petrarch, Dante, Copernicus, and Erasmus all studied there.

events.title: Council of Clermont
events.blurb: The pope, addressing a crowd of French clergy and nobles in an open field outside a central French city after a church council, called on Christendom to take up arms and march east to recover a holy land from Muslim rule. "Deus vult," the crowd cried back — "God wills it." Within three years, 100,000 pilgrims and knights would be on the road.
events.revealBlurb: November 27, 1095 — Pope Urban II. His stated goals shifted in each retelling; the Byzantine emperor had only asked for mercenaries. The First Crusade's armies would surprise everyone, including themselves, by actually reaching Jerusalem.

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Operation Barbarossa
events.blurb: Three million soldiers, 600,000 motorised vehicles, 3,600 tanks, and 2,700 aircraft crossed a 2,900-kilometre border in the pre-dawn darkness, launching the largest land invasion in military history. The defender's air force lost over a thousand planes in the first day, many of them still on the ground.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 1941. Stalin reportedly refused to believe his own border commanders' early reports and assumed the attacks were unauthorised provocations. The operation's codename referenced the medieval Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. By December, Germany had advanced 1,000 km but failed to knock the Soviet Union out of the war.

events.title: FDR's "Day of Infamy" Speech
events.blurb: A president delivered a 6-minute address to a joint session of his nation's legislature the morning after a surprise naval attack, opening with a phrase he had changed at the last moment from "world history" to something more damning, and closing with a request for a formal declaration of war that passed within hours with a single dissenting vote.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1941 — 81% of American adults listening by radio, the largest audience in broadcast history to that point. Congress voted 82-to-0 in the Senate, 388-to-1 in the House. The lone "no" vote, pacifist Jeannette Rankin of Montana, had also voted against entering World War I.

events.title: Japanese-American Internment
events.blurb: A presidential order authorised the forced removal of all people of a specific ethnic ancestry from the entire western coast of a country — regardless of citizenship — to inland camps surrounded by guard towers and barbed wire, without trial or individual evidence of wrongdoing. Roughly 122,000 people were displaced; two-thirds were native-born citizens.
events.revealBlurb: Executive Order 9066, signed February 19, 1942. The Supreme Court upheld it in 1944. In 1988, Congress formally apologised and paid $20,000 in reparations to each surviving detainee — roughly 82,000 people. A 2011 Department of Justice memo officially acknowledged the government's lawyers had hidden evidence of innocence from the original court.

events.title: Tehran Conference
events.blurb: The three most powerful leaders of the opposing alliance met for the first time in a capital city in southwest Asia, committing to a firm timeline for a massive cross-channel invasion in spring, agreeing on the postwar borders of one eastern European nation, and beginning to sketch the political shape of the world that would follow the conflict.
events.revealBlurb: November 28 – December 1, 1943 — FDR, Churchill, and Stalin met in Tehran. It was the first time FDR and Stalin met in person. Roosevelt, whose security staff feared assassination, moved into the Soviet Embassy at Stalin's suggestion — and Soviet intelligence promptly bugged his suite. Churchill celebrated his 69th birthday at the conference with a dinner attended by all three leaders.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: Seven Samurai Released
events.blurb: A Japanese director released a 207-minute epic about a defenseless farming village that hires seven masterless samurai to protect it from annual bandit raids. The film's action-adventure template — a diverse team of skilled specialists assembled for a dangerous mission — has been imitated in countless subsequent movies across every genre. One of its rainy climactic battles required 18 weeks of shooting and 500 tons of supplemental water.
