events.revealBlurb: April 26, 1954 — Akira Kurosawa, starring Toshiro Mifune. The film was remade by Hollywood six years later as "The Magnificent Seven." The 2016 Marvel film "The Avengers" has been called, by its own director, a direct descendant.

events.title: Breathless Released
events.blurb: A 29-year-old French film critic turned director released a 90-minute crime film about a petty thief on the run in Paris with his American girlfriend, shot on handheld camera using natural light, jump cuts, and improvised dialogue. The film's insouciant rulebreaking embodied a new generation of European filmmaking, christened the "Nouvelle Vague" by a critic five years earlier. It made its star into the archetype of post-war cool.
events.revealBlurb: March 16, 1960 — Jean-Luc Godard, starring Jean-Paul Belmondo and Jean Seberg. The famously jarring jump-cuts emerged from an editing crisis: the film was too long and Godard simply removed shots rather than shorten scenes.

events.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey Released
events.blurb: A 39-year-old New York-born director released a 149-minute science-fiction film about human evolution, artificial intelligence, and alien contact, with minimal dialogue, a four-movement structure, and long classical-music sequences of spacecraft slowly docking to the Blue Danube. The first audience walked out in droves; reviews were mixed. Within two years, it was the highest-grossing film of its year and had reshaped what cinema was permitted to do.
events.revealBlurb: April 2, 1968 — Stanley Kubrick. Co-written with Arthur C. Clarke. The jump cut from a primeval bone thrown into the air to a spaceship in orbit covers 4 million years in one frame. HAL 9000's voice was performed by Canadian Shakespearean actor Douglas Rain.

events.title: Toy Story Released
events.blurb: A California animation studio released the first feature film produced entirely with computer-generated imagery, a 81-minute buddy comedy about a child's cowboy doll who feels threatened by a new space-ranger action figure. The studio had spent four years on the film, through three near-cancellations and total rewrites; the resulting picture grossed $390 million and established a new production studio as the dominant force in animation for the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1995 — Pixar Animation Studios, directed by John Lasseter. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen voiced Woody and Buzz Lightyear. Pixar had been Apple founder Steve Jobs's expensive side-project; Disney bought them for $7.4 billion in 2006.

events.title: Pong Released in Arcades
events.blurb: A black-and-white rectangle containing two paddles and a bouncing dot was installed in a Sunnyvale, California tavern as a hardware test. The test machine broke within days — not from malfunction, but because the coin slot had overflowed with quarters. Atari scrambled to ship units nationwide, and the commercial video game industry was born.
events.revealBlurb: November 29, 1972 — Atari Inc., founded that June by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney, shipped Pong to arcades. The Andy Capp's Tavern prototype jammed after a week because it held too many coins.

events.title: Super Mario Bros. Released in Japan
events.blurb: A moustachioed Italian plumber leaping over mushrooms and sliding down pipes became the defining character of interactive entertainment. The game shipped as a pack-in with the Nintendo Entertainment System and single-handedly revived an industry that had collapsed two years earlier under the weight of its own shovelware.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 1985 — Super Mario Bros. launched for Nintendo's Famicom in Japan. It sold over 40 million copies, a record that stood until Wii Sports in 2009. Designer Shigeru Miyamoto built the entire world around the mechanic of a running jump.

events.title: Half-Life Released by Valve
events.blurb: Every first-person shooter before Half-Life presented missions as separate levels with loading screens and no coherent world. Half-Life placed the player inside a continuous unbroken environment, told its story entirely through actions the player participated in, and won more than 50 Game of the Year awards. Critics later divided gaming history into "pre-Half-Life" and "post-Half-Life" eras.
events.revealBlurb: November 19, 1998 — Valve's debut game released for Windows. Budgeted for lifetime sales of 180,000 copies, it sold 212,000 in the United States alone by year-end and ultimately over 9 million copies. It spawned Counter-Strike as a fan mod. Valve used the revenue to build Steam.

events.title: Counter-Strike Released as Standalone
events.blurb: Two amateur developers built a modification for Half-Life in which terrorists and counter-terrorists fought in small tactical maps. Valve noticed the mod's download numbers, purchased the rights, and released it as a standalone product. It became the most-played online game in the world for over a decade, the game credited with institutionalising competitive PC gaming.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 2000 — Counter-Strike version 1.0 released as a free Half-Life modification. Creators Minh "Gooseman" Le and Jess Cliffe had started the mod in June 1999. In 2023, CS:GO/CS2 peaked at over 1.8 million concurrent Steam players.

events.title: Pokémon GO Launches
events.blurb: A mobile game using GPS and augmented reality sent tens of millions of people into parks, cemeteries, and government buildings to catch fictional creatures on their phones. It broke multiple App Store records in its first 24 hours. Police stations issued public statements asking players not to enter. Central Park held impromptu gatherings of thousands at midnight.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 2016 — Pokémon GO launched in the United States, Australia, and New Zealand. It surpassed 100 million downloads in under 30 days and generated $207 million in its first month — the highest ever for a mobile game. Lifetime revenue has surpassed $6 billion.

events.title: Euclid's Elements Written
events.blurb: A 13-book mathematical treatise organised geometry, number theory, and proportion into a rigorous deductive system built from five simple axioms and five postulates, from which hundreds of theorems were derived by logical proof alone. The work became the model for mathematical reasoning for more than two thousand years and remained a standard university textbook in parts of Europe into the twentieth century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 300 BCE — almost nothing is known about Euclid himself; even his birthdate is unknown. The Elements is the second most-printed book in history after the Bible. One of its five postulates — the parallel postulate — resisted proof for two thousand years; mathematicians who tried to derive it instead invented non-Euclidean geometry.

events.title: Galileo Maps the Moon
events.blurb: An Italian natural philosopher directed a 20× magnification tube skyward and produced detailed drawings of the Moon's surface, revealing mountains and craters rather than a perfect celestial sphere as ancient philosophy held. He calculated the heights of lunar mountains by measuring the lengths of the shadows they cast.

events.title: On the Origin of Species Published
events.blurb: A 502-page book argued that all species of life descended from common ancestors through a process of natural selection, where individuals with heritable traits better suited to their environment survived and reproduced at higher rates. The first print run of 1,250 copies sold out to booksellers on the day it was offered for sale.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1859 — Darwin had sat on the theory for twenty years, terrified of the controversy. He finally rushed it to press only after Alfred Russel Wallace independently wrote him a letter describing the same mechanism. The two men's papers were presented jointly to the Linnean Society in 1858.

events.title: Pluto Discovered
events.blurb: A young farm-hand-turned-astronomer at an Arizona observatory found a faint, slowly moving point of light by comparing photographic plates taken several days apart — a new body at the edge of the solar system. The discovery completed a decadelong search for a hypothetical ninth planet believed to be perturbing the orbits of the outermost known worlds.
events.revealBlurb: February 18, 1930 — Clyde Tombaugh was 24 and had never attended university. The name "Pluto" was suggested by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl in Oxford, via her grandfather. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a "dwarf planet," prompting widespread public outrage and several state legislatures to pass resolutions disagreeing.

events.title: Endosymbiotic Theory Published
events.blurb: A paper proposed that the energy-producing mitochondria and photosynthetic chloroplasts inside complex cells were originally free-living bacteria that had been engulfed by a host cell and retained over billions of years — a radical claim that the cell's most vital structures were once independent organisms. The paper had been rejected by approximately fifteen journals before finding a publisher.
events.revealBlurb: June 1967 — Lynn Margulis submitted the paper under her married surname Sagan; it became one of biology's most-cited papers after decades of derision. Her critics called it "too fantastic." When the hypothesis was tested by comparing DNA in mitochondria to bacterial DNA in the 1980s, it matched almost exactly.

events.title: Mosaic Browser Released
events.blurb: Undergraduate students at a University of Illinois supercomputing centre released a graphical web browser for Unix, with a version for Windows and Mac released later in the year. Unlike the earlier terminal-based browsers, it could display images inline with text. Within 18 months, web traffic had grown by 10,000 percent. The browser's lead developer would leave to co-found a company that would dominate the next phase.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1993 — developed at the NCSA, lead developer Marc Andreessen. Andreessen co-founded Netscape within a year. Mosaic was free for non-commercial use, a decision that gave the web the critical mass it needed.

events.title: Yahoo! Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford electrical engineering PhD students who had spent a year maintaining a website called "Jerry and David's guide to the World Wide Web" — a manually curated directory of interesting sites — incorporated their hobby as a business. They'd rename it with a word from Gulliver's Travels meaning an uncouth, rude person. For most of the decade, it was the default homepage of the internet.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1995 — Jerry Yang and David Filo. The name is officially a backronym: "Yet Another Hierarchical Officious Oracle." They turned down a $44.6 billion acquisition offer from Microsoft in 2008; Verizon eventually bought the husk for $4.48 billion in 2017.

events.title: Instagram Launched
events.blurb: A two-person startup released a free iOS app that let users take photos, apply one of eleven retro filters, and share them to a simple timeline-based social network. It acquired 25,000 users on launch day and its first million within three months. Facebook bought the company for $1 billion in cash and stock eighteen months later, when it had thirteen employees and zero revenue.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 2010 — Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. Originally built as a location-based check-in app called Burbn. The $1 billion Facebook acquisition in April 2012 is now considered one of the great bargains in tech history.

events.title: WikiLeaks Cablegate
events.blurb: A whistleblower-platform website and a consortium of five newspapers began publishing, in coordinated waves, 251,287 U.S. diplomatic cables leaked by a 22-year-old U.S. Army intelligence analyst. The cables ranged from the mundane to the explosive — unflattering private assessments of world leaders, evidence of corruption in allied governments, and revelations about civilian deaths in Iraq and Afghanistan. The leaker would face the longest sentence ever imposed for leaking U.S. government information.
events.revealBlurb: November 28, 2010 — leaker Chelsea Manning (then Bradley), sentenced to 35 years in 2013. Obama commuted her sentence in 2017. WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange lived in the Ecuadorian embassy in London from 2012 until 2019; he was released from UK custody in a 2024 plea deal.

events.title: ChatGPT Launched
events.blurb: A San Francisco AI research lab released, as an unassuming "research preview," a conversational interface to its large language model. The chatbot could answer questions, write essays, debug code, and generate poetry in response to natural-language prompts. It gained a hundred million monthly users within two months — making it the fastest-growing consumer product in history. Incumbent tech giants pivoted their entire product strategies within weeks.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 2022 — OpenAI. The underlying model, GPT-3.5, had existed for months; the chat wrapper made all the difference. By 2025, generative AI had become a ~$200 billion global industry. Anthropic, Google, Meta, and xAI joined OpenAI as frontier labs.

events.title: Quit India Movement
events.blurb: After the failure of a British mission that offered only a vague promise of post-war dominion status, the Congress party launched a mass movement demanding immediate British withdrawal. The entire leadership was arrested at dawn the following day. The movement went underground and continued for years — sabotage, strikes, alternative governments in remote districts. It was violently suppressed, but British rule was visibly over as a legitimate proposition.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 1942 — Gandhi's "Do or Die" speech at the Bombay Congress session. Churchill imprisoned 100,000 activists and held the line; by VJ Day in 1945, however, Britain was bankrupt and the political capital to hold India was gone.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Emergency Declared
events.blurb: Two weeks after a court had found her guilty of electoral malpractice and barred her from office, a prime minister persuaded the president to declare a state of emergency under the constitution. Opposition leaders were arrested in the night, press censorship imposed, civil liberties suspended, and constitutional amendments rushed through a pliant parliament. The suspension of democracy lasted 21 months and is the darkest interval in the republic's history.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1975 — Indira Gandhi. The Emergency was defended in the name of stability; mass sterilizations, slum clearances, and the personality cult of her son Sanjay made it notorious. Ended March 21, 1977.

events.title: Kargil War
events.blurb: Pakistani soldiers, disguised as local insurgents, occupied high-altitude ridges inside the Indian-administered portion of a disputed northern territory over the winter. Their discovery by a shepherd in early May touched off a 74-day war fought at elevations up to 5,600 metres. India retook the peaks one by one with heavy infantry losses; Pakistan, pressured by Washington, withdrew.
events.revealBlurb: May 3 to July 26, 1999 — the Line of Control in Kargil, Ladakh. The conflict was one of the first televised wars in India. Captain Vikram Batra became a national hero before dying on Point 4875 on July 7.

events.title: 26/11 Mumbai Attacks
events.blurb: Ten men trained by a Pakistan-based militant group landed at a fishing harbour in the country's financial capital by rubber dinghy after hijacking an Indian fishing trawler at sea, and fanned out across the city to attack a railway station, a Jewish centre, a café, and two luxury hotels. The resulting sieges lasted 60 hours. 166 people died and more than 300 were wounded. Nine attackers were killed; the sole survivor was captured, tried, and hanged four years later.
events.revealBlurb: November 26-29, 2008 — Mumbai. The captured gunman, Ajmal Kasab, was hanged on November 21, 2012. The attacks were coordinated over satellite phone from Karachi; the operational planner, Sajid Mir, was finally convicted in Pakistan in 2022.

events.title: Nightingale at Scutari
events.blurb: A 34-year-old British nurse arrived with 38 volunteer nurses at a filthy military hospital in a former Turkish barracks outside a Bosphorus capital, where British wounded from a Crimean war were dying of typhus, cholera, and dysentery at far higher rates than from combat wounds. Her reforms — sanitation, proper food, hand-washing, laundry — cut the death rate from 42 percent to 2 percent in six months. Her subsequent statistical advocacy reshaped nursing as a profession.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 1854 — Florence Nightingale at Scutari (now Üsküdar, Istanbul). Her nighttime rounds with an oil lamp produced the "Lady with the Lamp" sobriquet. She returned to London with chronic brucellosis, spent most of the rest of her life bedridden, and still wrote 200 books and reports. She lived to 90.

events.title: Koch Identifies TB Bacillus
events.blurb: A 38-year-old German physician, presenting to the Berlin Physiological Society, announced he had isolated and cultured the bacillus responsible for tuberculosis — a disease that killed roughly one in seven people in 19th-century Europe. He had developed systematic protocols — now called Koch's postulates — for identifying which microbes caused which diseases. He would identify the cholera bacillus two years later.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1882 — Robert Koch. World Tuberculosis Day is commemorated on this anniversary each year. Koch won the Nobel Prize in 1905. His attempted TB vaccine, tuberculin, was a failure — but became a useful skin test for TB exposure.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: First Human Heart Transplant
events.blurb: A South African surgeon transplanted the heart of a 25-year-old accident victim into a 53-year-old grocer in a nine-hour operation at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town. The recipient survived 18 days before dying of pneumonia; the same surgical team performed a second transplant 13 days later — that patient lived 19 months.

events.title: First Heart Transplant
events.blurb: A South African surgeon led a nine-hour operation at a Cape Town hospital transplanting the heart of a 25-year-old woman, killed by a car striking her as she crossed the road to buy cake, into the chest of a 54-year-old man with severe coronary disease. The patient lived 18 days before dying of pneumonia. The surgeon instantly became internationally famous; subsequent transplant patients lived increasingly long with improved immunosuppression.
events.revealBlurb: December 3, 1967 — Christiaan Barnard at Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town. Patient: Louis Washkansky. Donor: Denise Darvall. Barnard's second patient, Philip Blaiberg, lived 19 months. The 5-year survival rate for heart transplants is now about 75 percent.

events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: Napoleon Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Corsican-born general, having ruled France as First Consul for five years, staged a coronation at the Gothic cathedral in the French capital. He had negotiated the pope's attendance; in the ceremony's most famous moment — possibly prearranged, possibly improvised — the emperor took the crown from the pope and placed it on his own head. The act was read as a message: no religious authority ratified his power.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1804 — Notre-Dame de Paris. Pope Pius VII had been brought from Rome; he sat largely passive through the ceremony. Napoleon's wife Joséphine also crowned herself empress. Jacques-Louis David's monumental painting of the coronation, finished three years later, flatters Napoleon's height among other details.

events.title: Battle of Austerlitz
events.blurb: A French army of 68,000 men, outnumbered by a combined Russian and Austrian force of 89,000, achieved what is still regarded as one of the greatest tactical victories in military history. Feigning weakness, the French commander baited his opponents into attacking his deliberately weakened right flank, then counter-attacked through the centre as the enemy's lines stretched thin. Three emperors had taken the field; two retreated; the Holy Roman Empire would formally dissolve within a year.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1805 — Napoleon's victory over Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II, on the first anniversary of his coronation. The battle is also called "the Battle of the Three Emperors." Allied casualties: ~36,000. French: ~9,000.

events.title: 1830 July Revolution
events.blurb: A French king's attempt to restore near-absolutist rule by restrictive decrees — censoring the press, dissolving the chamber of deputies — provoked three days of street fighting in the French capital. Parisian artisans, workers, and students threw up barricades; the king fled the country. A constitutional monarchy was installed under a cousin, the "Citizen King," who agreed to govern as a bourgeois rather than divine monarch. Delacroix's painting of "Liberty Leading the People" commemorated it.
events.revealBlurb: July 27-29, 1830 — "Les Trois Glorieuses." Deposed king: Charles X. Successor: Louis-Philippe of the Orléans cadet branch. Delacroix's painting was completed within months and exhibited at the 1831 Paris Salon.

events.title: Revolutions of 1848
events.blurb: Political unrest that had been gathering over economic recession and demands for constitutional government erupted within weeks across most of the European continent, beginning with a winter insurrection in Paris that deposed the king. Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest, Prague, and a dozen other capitals followed within months. Liberals, nationalists, socialists, and workers briefly shared rhetoric; conservatives reorganized and, over the following year, crushed nearly every revolt. The conservative order emerged apparently reinforced — but the political grammar of 19th-century Europe had changed.
events.revealBlurb: February-June 1848 — "The Springtime of Nations." Louis-Philippe of France fled in February; Metternich resigned in Vienna in March. Only France produced lasting regime change, and it soon produced Napoleon III's Second Empire. Karl Marx and Engels published the Communist Manifesto that same February.

events.title: 13th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: The first of three Reconstruction-era amendments was ratified eight months after a brutal civil war ended, abolishing slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States except as punishment for crime. The exception clause would become the legal scaffolding for convict-leasing systems that reproduced plantation labor for another 80 years.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1865 — when Georgia became the 27th state to ratify. Mississippi officially ratified only in 1995, and didn't certify it until 2013, due to a paperwork oversight.

events.title: Military Desegregation Order
events.blurb: A U.S. president signed an executive order mandating "equality of treatment and opportunity" in the armed forces without regard to race, color, religion, or national origin. The army resisted for nearly five years; full integration of combat units was not achieved until the Korean War made ignoring Black replacements impossible.
events.revealBlurb: July 26, 1948 — Executive Order 9981, Harry Truman. He signed it partly out of conviction, partly because Black voters in northern cities were now pivotal to Democratic victory. The last all-Black unit was dissolved in 1954.

events.title: Rosa Parks Arrested
events.blurb: A 42-year-old department-store seamstress and longtime NAACP secretary refused to give up her seat on a city bus in an Alabama capital when the white section filled up and the driver demanded the first row of Black seating. She was arrested for violating municipal segregation ordinances. The local Black community organized a one-day bus boycott that became a 381-day boycott.
events.revealBlurb: December 1, 1955 — Montgomery, Alabama. Parks was not, as legend has it, "too tired" to move — she was a trained activist who had attended a civil rights training school months earlier. Her act was calculated. A 26-year-old new preacher in town, Martin Luther King Jr., was chosen to lead the boycott.

events.title: Greensboro Sit-Ins
events.blurb: Four Black college freshmen sat down at the segregated lunch counter of a downtown variety store in a North Carolina city and politely ordered coffee. When refused service, they stayed seated until closing. They returned the next day with more students. Within two months, similar sit-ins had spread to 55 cities in 13 states, and the variety-store chain desegregated its counters.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 1960 — Woolworth's lunch counter, Greensboro. The original four were students at North Carolina A&T State University: Ezell Blair, Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil, David Richmond. Part of the counter is now in the Smithsonian.

events.title: Freedom Riders Depart
events.blurb: Thirteen volunteers — seven Black, six white — boarded buses in Washington, D.C. bound for New Orleans to test a recent Supreme Court ruling outlawing segregated interstate travel facilities. In Alabama their bus was firebombed outside Anniston and the riders beaten bloody by a mob in Birmingham. They kept riding. Subsequent waves continued through the summer.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1961 — sponsored by CORE. A 21-year-old John Lewis was among them and had his skull fractured. Attorney General Robert Kennedy called for a "cooling-off period;" CORE leader James Farmer replied: "We've been cooling off for 100 years."

events.title: Galileo Observes the Moon Through a Telescope
events.blurb: Turning a new optical instrument toward the night sky, an Italian mathematician observed that the Moon's surface was rough, mountainous, and marked by craters — directly contradicting the ancient belief that celestial bodies were perfect smooth spheres. Careful drawings of the shadow lines allowed him to estimate the height of lunar mountains by triangulating shadow lengths.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 1609 — Galileo had only heard a description of a Dutch spyglass and built his own without ever seeing one. His 1610 pamphlet Sidereus Nuncius went through its entire print run within a week. He dedicated Jupiter's four moons to the Medici family to secure patronage — an early example of branded science.

events.title: Helium Detected in the Sun
events.blurb: During a total solar eclipse, a French astronomer studying the spectrum of light from the Sun's outer atmosphere found a bright yellow spectral line that matched no known element on Earth, suggesting the existence of a new element present in the Sun but not yet found on our planet. Two months later, an English astronomer independently identified the same line and gave the element its name, derived from the Greek word for the Sun.
events.revealBlurb: August 18, 1868 — Janssen realised during the eclipse that the bright chromospheric lines could be observed in daylight without an eclipse and invented the spectroscope for doing so. Helium was not detected on Earth for another 27 years, when it was found in a uranium mineral in 1895. It is the only element discovered in space before being found on Earth.

events.title: Special Relativity Paper Published
events.blurb: A 30-page paper demolished the concept of absolute time, arguing that the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of their motion, and that simultaneity, length, and mass all depend on relative velocity. The paper contained no citations, because its author — a patent clerk working in his spare time — had arrived at the theory by pure thought experiment.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1905 — one of four papers the same author submitted to Annalen der Physik that year, including one on Brownian motion and one that would later win the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect. The mass-energy equivalence paper (E=mc²) followed two months later.

events.title: Pulsars Discovered
events.blurb: A graduate student mapping the sky with a radio telescope noticed a repeating pulse of radio waves arriving with uncanny regularity every 1.33 seconds — far too precise to be natural noise. The signal was briefly nicknamed "LGM-1" (Little Green Men) until other examples were found across the sky, establishing a new class of rapidly rotating neutron stars more accurate than any clock then built.
events.revealBlurb: November 28, 1967 — Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted the anomaly in paper chart rolls she had to check by hand. Her supervisor Antony Hewish and astronomer Martin Ryle shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery; Bell Burnell was excluded despite being the one who found it, in what became one of science's most-debated Nobel omissions.

events.title: CRISPR-Cas9 Gene Editing Described
events.blurb: A paper in Science demonstrated that a bacterial immune system could be reprogrammed as a precise molecular tool to cut DNA at any chosen location in any genome, using a short guide RNA to direct a protein scissors to the exact target sequence. The technique was accurate, cheap, and fast compared to all previous gene-editing methods, immediately launching a revolution in biology.
events.revealBlurb: June 28, 2012 — Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier published the mechanism after Doudna had a nightmare in which Hitler asked her to explain the tool's potential uses. They shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. A bitter priority dispute erupted with the Broad Institute's Feng Zhang over who had actually first demonstrated editing in human cells.
